stem: Mira stores the studio’s name in a variable and prints it. Type what the command prints.
explanation: Inside double quotes the shell still expands variables, and single quotes are ordinary characters there. So both `$x` become `Pixel`, and the single quotes are printed as they are. Only single quotes on the outside would stop the expansion.

stem: Jonas wonders whether `cd` is a program in `/usr/bin` or part of Bash itself. Which command, followed by `cd`, answers that? Type the command name.
explanation: `type cd` prints `cd is a shell builtin`, while `type tar` prints the path of the executable, such as `/usr/bin/tar`. Builtins like `cd` have to live inside the shell, because a separate program can’t change the shell’s working directory.

stem: Jonas types a line into his terminal window. Which program reads that line, works out the command in it and starts the right program?

options.text: The kernel, which parses the text and runs it by itself
options.rationale: The kernel runs programs, but it does not read or interpret command lines; the shell does that.

options.text: The terminal emulator, which looks up each command name
options.rationale: The terminal window only shows text and passes keystrokes on; it does not interpret commands.

options.text: The shell, which on most distributions is Bash
options.rationale: The shell reads and interprets every line; Bash is the usual default.

options.text: The init system, which launches every command typed
options.rationale: The init system starts system services at boot, not the commands a user types.

explanation: The terminal is only a window. The shell, usually Bash, reads each line, splits it into words, expands variables and wildcards and then asks the kernel to start the program.

stem: What does the name “Bash” stand for?

options.rationale: It is a pun on the older Bourne shell, which Bash replaced and extended.
No such expansion exists, and Bash is not limited to administrators.
Bash has nothing to do with binary access; it is a command interpreter.
Berkeley produced other shells, but Bash comes from the GNU project.

explanation: Bash is the GNU project’s “Bourne Again SHell”, a successor to the original Bourne shell. It is the default login shell on most Linux distributions.

stem: Mira types `cd pro` and presses the Tab key. Only one name in the current directory starts with `pro`. What happens?

options.text: Bash inserts a tab character into the command line
options.rationale: In an interactive shell, Tab is bound to completion, not to a literal tab character.

options.text: Bash runs `cd` with the text `pro` as the directory
options.rationale: Nothing runs until Enter is pressed, and Tab only completes the word.

options.text: Bash lists every file in the directory and runs nothing
options.rationale: A list of choices appears only when several names match, not when exactly one does.

options.text: Bash completes the name, for example to `projects/`
options.rationale: Tab completion fills in the rest of a name when only one match exists.

explanation: Tab asks Bash to complete the word under the cursor. One match is filled in at once; several matches are shown after a second Tab press. It saves typing and avoids typos.

stem: A command Ada started is still running and she wants to stop it from the keyboard. Which key combination sends it an interrupt?

options.rationale: Ctrl+D signals the end of input; at an empty prompt it closes the shell, but it does not interrupt a program.
Ctrl+C interrupts the foreground program.
Ctrl+L clears the terminal screen and leaves the program running.
Ctrl+R searches the command history; it does not stop anything.

explanation: Ctrl+C sends an interrupt to the program in the foreground. Ctrl+D ends input, Ctrl+L clears the screen and Ctrl+R searches the history.

stem: In the command `ls -l /srv/assets`, which part is the option?

options.rationale: This is the command name, the program being run.
Options start with a dash and change what the command does; `-l` asks for the long format.
This is an argument: the thing the command works on.
The command and its option together are not “the option”.

explanation: A command line has the command name first, then options that start with a dash, then arguments such as file or directory names. Here `ls` is the command, `-l` the option and `/srv/assets` the argument.

stem: Mira types `ls     -l      art` with several spaces between the words. How does Bash treat them?

options.text: It passes the extra spaces to `ls` as part of the arguments
options.rationale: Unquoted blanks only separate words; they are not passed on.

options.text: It reports a syntax error because of the repeated spaces
options.rationale: Repeated blanks are allowed and ignored between words.

options.text: It runs `ls` three times, once for each group of spaces
options.rationale: Spaces never cause a command to repeat; the line is one command.

options.text: It treats each run of spaces as one separator and passes three words
options.rationale: The shell splits the line into words at blanks, so extra spaces make no difference.

explanation: Bash splits the line into words at unquoted spaces and tabs. How many blanks sit between the words doesn’t matter, which is why spaces inside a value have to be quoted to survive.

stem: Which character lets a single command line run two commands, one after the other, whether or not the first one succeeds?

options.rationale: A semicolon ends one command and starts the next, regardless of the first command’s result.
A pipe sends the output of the first command into the second; they run together.
A hash turns the rest of the line into a comment, so nothing after it runs.
The second command runs only if the first one succeeds.

explanation: Use `;` to put several commands on one line. `&&` makes the second depend on the first’s success, `|` connects them through a pipe and `#` starts a comment.

stem: In Bash, what does a `#` at the start of a word do?

options.text: It runs the rest of the line as the administrator
options.rationale: The root prompt often ends in `#`, but typing it does not raise privileges.

options.text: It refers to the previous command in the history
options.rationale: History expansion uses `!`, not `#`.

options.text: Everything from there to the end of the line is a comment and is ignored
options.rationale: In an interactive shell Bash treats the rest of the line as a comment.

options.text: It expands to the number of arguments given
options.rationale: The number of arguments is `$#`, which is a different use of the character.

explanation: A `#` that begins a word starts a comment. Scripts use it for notes and for the first line `#!/bin/bash`. Don’t confuse it with the root prompt, which ends in `#` only as a display convention.

stem: Which of these is the long form of the `-a` option of `ls`?

options.rationale: With a single dash this means the options `-a`, `-l` and `-l` combined, not a long option.
This option does not exist in `ls`.
GNU tools pair many short options with a long form; `ls --all` equals `ls -a`.
That is the long form of `-A`, which leaves out `.` and `..`.

explanation: Long options start with two dashes and use whole words. A single dash followed by several letters is a bundle of short options, so `-all` is not a long option.

stem: Mira runs `level=3` in her terminal and then starts a new `bash` from it. Inside the new shell, `echo $level` prints nothing. Why?

options.text: `level` is a shell variable that was never exported, so child processes don’t inherit it
options.rationale: Only exported variables are copied into the environment of programs started from the shell.

options.text: Variable names must be written in upper case to be inherited
options.rationale: The name’s case is irrelevant to inheritance; `export` is what matters.

options.text: The variable was erased as soon as the line ended
options.rationale: The variable lives until the shell exits; it just isn’t passed on.

options.text: The assignment is a comment because it has no quotes
options.rationale: Assignments without quotes are fine, and a comment needs a `#`.

explanation: A plain assignment creates a variable that exists only in the current shell. `export level` (or `export level=3`) puts it in the environment, which every child process inherits.

stem: The variable `GAME` already exists in Ada’s shell. Which command makes it visible to the programs she starts from this shell?

options.rationale: This prints the word GAME; it changes nothing.
`type` describes commands, not variables.
`history` lists earlier command lines and doesn’t export anything.
`export` marks the variable for the environment of child processes.

explanation: `export NAME` marks an existing variable for export, and `export NAME=value` sets and exports it in one step. Without export, the variable stays local to the shell.

stem: Which line correctly assigns the value `Pixel` to the variable `title` in Bash?

options.rationale: With spaces, Bash tries to run a command named `title` with two arguments.
An assignment has no spaces around the equals sign.
The dollar sign is used to read a variable, not to name it in an assignment.
`set` doesn’t create a variable this way; it would set positional parameters instead.

explanation: In Bash an assignment is `NAME=value` with no spaces on either side of the `=`. The `$` is only written when you read the value.

stem: What does the `PATH` environment variable contain?

options.text: The absolute path of the directory you are currently in
options.rationale: That is the job of `PWD`, not `PATH`.

options.text: A colon-separated list of directories in which the shell looks for commands
options.rationale: When you type a name without a slash, Bash searches these directories in order.

options.text: A space-separated list of the files you opened recently
options.rationale: The shell keeps no such list; recent commands live in the history.

options.text: The location of the user’s home directory
options.rationale: That is the `HOME` variable.

explanation: `PATH` is a list of directories separated by colons, such as `/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin`. The shell tries each one from left to right and runs the first match it finds.

stem: Mira put a script called `deploy` in her current directory. Typing `deploy` gives “command not found”, but `./deploy` works. What explains this?

options.text: Scripts can only be run when their names begin with a dot and a slash
options.rationale: The `./` is just a path to the file; the file’s name doesn’t need to include it.

options.text: The shell only runs files whose names end in `.sh`
options.rationale: Bash doesn’t require any extension; the executable permission matters.

options.text: The script must be exported with `export` before it can run
options.rationale: `export` is for variables, not for programs.

options.text: The current directory isn’t listed in `PATH`, so the shell doesn’t search it
options.rationale: A name without a slash is only looked up in the `PATH` directories; `./` names the file explicitly.

explanation: Without a slash, Bash searches only the directories in `PATH`. Giving a path, such as `./deploy` or `/home/mira/deploy`, skips the search. The current directory is left out of `PATH` on purpose, for safety.

stem: Which Bash builtin reports whether a name such as `echo` is a builtin, an alias, a keyword or a program found through `PATH`?

options.rationale: `type NAME` describes how Bash would interpret that name.
`history` lists earlier command lines.
`export` marks variables for child processes.
`read` reads a line of input into a variable.

explanation: `type echo` prints “echo is a shell builtin”, while `type ls` prints the path of the executable file. `type -t NAME` prints only one word: `builtin`, `file`, `alias` or `keyword`.

stem: Why can `cd` not be implemented as an ordinary program file like `ls`?

options.text: Programs on disk may not use directory names
options.rationale: Programs can read directories freely; that is not the reason.

options.text: `cd` is too small to be stored as a file
options.rationale: Size has nothing to do with it; plenty of tiny programs exist.

options.text: A separate program runs in its own process and could not change the working directory of the shell that started it
options.rationale: A working directory belongs to a process, so only the shell itself can change its own.

options.text: Only commands starting with a letter c can be builtins
options.rationale: Builtins can have any name, such as `echo` or `type`.

explanation: Each process has its own working directory. If `cd` were a separate program, it would change only its own directory and then exit, leaving the shell where it was. That’s why `cd` is built into the shell.

stem: Which kind of quotes lets Bash expand `$name` inside the quoted text, while keeping the spaces in the text together as one word?

options.rationale: Single quotes keep every character literal, so `$name` would not be expanded.
Without quotes, the value is expanded but split at spaces into several words.
Inside double quotes, variables are expanded and the whole text stays one word.

options.text: A backslash in front of every space
options.rationale: A backslash escapes one character; it doesn’t make variables expand any differently.

explanation: Double quotes protect spaces but still allow `$` expansion. Single quotes switch off all special meanings, and without quotes the shell splits the result at spaces.

stem: What does a backslash in front of a character, as in `\$`, do in Bash?

options.text: It removes the special meaning of the next character
options.rationale: The backslash escapes exactly one character, which is then taken literally.

options.text: It starts a comment that runs to the end of the line
options.rationale: Comments begin with `#`.

options.text: It turns the next word into a variable name
options.rationale: Variables are introduced by `$`, not by a backslash.
The history uses `!!` for that.

explanation: The backslash is the escape character: `echo \$HOME` prints `$HOME` literally. At the very end of a line it also continues the command on the next line.

stem: Why is `echo "Mira’s level"` valid, while the same text in single quotes, `echo 'Mira's level'`, is not?

options.text: Double quotes allow apostrophes to be spelled with a backslash only
options.rationale: No backslash is needed inside double quotes here.

options.text: Single quotes may only contain digits and no words
options.rationale: Single-quoted text can hold any characters except a single quote.

options.text: Bash always refuses text that has an apostrophe in it
options.rationale: An apostrophe works fine as long as it is inside double quotes or escaped.

options.text: Inside single quotes, a single quote ends the quoted text; inside double quotes it is an ordinary character
options.rationale: Single quotes can’t contain a single quote, whereas double quotes treat it literally.

explanation: Single quotes end at the next single quote, no matter what. To print an apostrophe, put the text in double quotes or escape it with a backslash outside quotes.

stem: What does the `history` command show?

options.text: A list of the directories visited with `cd`
options.rationale: Bash’s history stores command lines, not directories.

options.text: A numbered list of the commands entered earlier in this shell
options.rationale: Bash remembers the lines you typed and numbers them, oldest first.

options.text: The manual pages read during the session
options.rationale: No record of manual pages is kept by `history`.

options.text: The files changed on the system today
options.rationale: File changes aren’t recorded by the shell history.

explanation: `history` prints the remembered command lines with numbers. `!!` repeats the last one, `!42` repeats line 42, and Bash saves the list in `~/.bash_history` when the shell exits.

stem: Under `/usr`, which directory holds programs mainly meant for system administration, such as tools that manage disks or users?

options.rationale: This holds the ordinary programs and commands for all users.
The `sbin` directories hold system administration programs, mainly for root.
This holds architecture-independent data such as documentation, not programs.
This holds libraries and supporting files, not the commands themselves.

explanation: Ordinary commands live in `/bin` and `/usr/bin`, while `/sbin` and `/usr/sbin` hold system administration programs. On a modern Debian system `/bin` and `/sbin` are links into `/usr`.

stem: Which directory, besides `/usr/bin`, traditionally holds the essential user commands such as `ls` and `cp`?

options.rationale: This holds configuration files, not programs.
This holds users’ personal files and directories.
This holds variable data such as logs and caches.
The FHS puts commands needed by all users in `/bin`.

explanation: `/bin` holds essential user commands. On current distributions it is usually a symbolic link to `/usr/bin`, so both paths reach the same programs.

stem: Which of these are builtin commands of Bash? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: It changes the shell’s own working directory, so it must be built in.
This is an external program, found as `/usr/bin/ls`.
It is a builtin that describes how a name would be run.
This is an external program.
This is an external program.

explanation: Builtins such as `cd` and `type` are part of Bash. `ls`, `cp` and `mkdir` are separate programs found through `PATH`. `type NAME` tells you which kind a command is.

stem: Which of these lines create a variable named `game` with the value `pixel`? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: A plain assignment with no spaces creates a shell variable.
The spaces make Bash run `game` as a command.
This assigns the value and also exports the variable.
The `$` would expand a variable first, so this is not an assignment.
Bash has no `var` keyword.

explanation: Both a plain assignment and `export NAME=value` create the variable; only the latter also puts it in the environment. Spaces around `=` break the assignment.

stem: Which commands print the text `$HOME` literally instead of the home directory? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: Single quotes switch off expansion.
Double quotes still expand variables.
Without quotes, the variable is expanded.
The backslash removes the special meaning of the dollar sign.
The parentheses are a syntax error in this position, and the variable would be expanded anyway.

explanation: To stop expansion, quote with single quotes or escape the `$` with a backslash. Double quotes and no quotes both expand `$HOME`.

stem: Which of these directories hold executable programs according to the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard? (Choose THREE.)

options.rationale: The main directory for user commands.
System administration programs.
Essential system administration programs.
Configuration files are kept here, not programs.
Users’ personal files, not system programs.

explanation: Commands are kept in `/bin`, `/usr/bin`, `/sbin` and `/usr/sbin`. `/etc` holds configuration and `/home` the users’ files.

stem: In `ls -l -a /srv`, which words are options? (Choose TWO.)

options.rationale: An option beginning with a dash.
The command name.
An option beginning with a dash.
An argument naming the directory to list.
This is a command with its first option, not a single word.

explanation: The first word is the command, words starting with a dash are options and the rest are arguments. `-l -a` could also be written `-la`.

stem: Which statements about the `PATH` variable are true? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Its directories are separated by colons
options.rationale: The entries are separated by `:`.

options.text: The shell searches its directories from left to right and runs the first match
options.rationale: The first directory containing the command wins.

options.text: Its directories are separated by spaces
options.rationale: Spaces would split the value into several words; colons are used.

options.text: It holds the directory you are in now
options.rationale: That is `PWD`.

options.text: Changing it in one terminal window changes it in all windows at once
options.rationale: Each shell has its own copy of its variables.

explanation: `PATH` is a colon-separated list that Bash walks through from the left. If two directories hold a command with the same name, the one listed first runs.

stem: Which builtin lists the commands you typed earlier, with numbers? Type the command.
explanation: `history` prints the numbered list of earlier lines. `!!` repeats the last one and `!N` repeats line N.

stem: Mira wants the variable `GAME` with the value `pixel` to be visible to programs started from her shell. Type one command that sets and exports it.
explanation: `export GAME=pixel` assigns the value and marks the variable for the environment in one step. A plain `GAME=pixel` stays local to the shell.

stem: Use `echo` to print the value of the `PATH` variable. Type the command.
explanation: A dollar sign in front of the variable name makes the shell replace it with its value. `echo "$PATH"` works too; the quotes are optional here.

stem: Type the `echo` command that prints exactly `$HOME`, using single quotes.
explanation: Inside single quotes nothing is expanded, so `$HOME` is printed as typed.

stem: Type the absolute path of the directory under `/usr` that holds programs for system administration.
explanation: `/usr/sbin` holds administration programs. Ordinary user commands are in `/usr/bin`.

stem: Finish the command so that the variable is passed on to child processes.
explanation: `export LEVEL=3` creates the variable and exports it. Remember there are no spaces around the `=`.

stem: Type the name of the variable (without a dollar sign) that lists the directories Bash searches for programs.
explanation: The variable is `PATH`. Its directories are separated by colons and searched from left to right.

stem: Type the name of the variable (without a dollar sign) that holds the path of the current user’s home directory.
explanation: `HOME` holds the home directory, such as `/home/mira`. The `~` shortcut expands to the same place.

stem: Type an `echo` command that prints the word Raiders without adding a newline afterwards.
explanation: The `-n` option of `echo` leaves out the trailing newline, so the next prompt would appear right after the word.

stem: Mira stores a name in a variable and greets it. Type what the command prints.
explanation: Double quotes still allow `$name` to be expanded, so the text `Hello, Mira` is printed.

stem: Jonas tries the same greeting with single quotes. What does this command print?

options.rationale: Single quotes keep every character literal, so `$name` is printed as it is.
This would need double quotes, which expand the variable.
The dollar sign is kept, so the variable name is not reduced to plain text.
An empty value would only appear if the variable were unset and expanded.

explanation: Single quotes turn off all expansion. The shell passes `Hello, $name` to `echo` unchanged.

stem: Ada types extra spaces between the words. What does this command print?

options.rationale: The shell splits unquoted text at blanks, so the extra spaces are lost.
`echo` puts a single space between its arguments.
The shell splits the line into three words and `echo` prints them separated by single spaces.
Nothing in the shell replaces spaces with underscores.

explanation: Unquoted blanks only separate words. To keep the extra spaces, quote the text.

stem: Now the same kind of spacing, but inside double quotes. Type what the command prints.
explanation: Quotes make the text a single word, so `echo` receives it with all six spaces and prints them.

stem: Mira sets `x` without exporting it and then starts a new `bash` that prints it. What does the command print?

options.rationale: That would need the variable exported; the child shell never received it.
Nothing turns the variable name into text.
The variable is local to the first shell, so the child sees an empty value and prints just the brackets.
The inner shell expands `$x` inside double quotes; the text is not printed literally.

explanation: A variable that has not been exported isn’t in the environment of child processes. The inner Bash expands `$x` to nothing.

stem: This time Mira exports the variable first. Type what the command prints.
explanation: `export` puts `x` into the environment, so the child shell inherits it and prints `[5]`.

stem: A price must show a literal dollar sign. What does this command print?

options.rationale: Inside double quotes, `\$` yields a literal `$`, so the text appears unchanged without the backslash.
The backslash escapes the dollar sign, so it stays in the output.
Inside double quotes `\$` becomes a plain `$`; the backslash is removed.
Without the backslash, `$5` would be expanded to an empty value; here it is escaped.

explanation: A backslash in front of `$` stops the expansion, even inside double quotes, and is removed afterwards.

stem: What does this command print?

options.rationale: A program with that name exists, but Bash prefers its builtin.

options.text: echo is an alias for printf
options.rationale: No alias is defined for it.
`echo` is known to the shell, so this error doesn’t appear.
`type` reports builtins first, and `echo` is built into Bash.

explanation: Bash has its own `echo`, which is found before any file in `PATH`. `type -a echo` would also list the files with that name.

stem: Type what the command prints.
explanation: The first `echo` has `-n`, so it prints no newline; the second word follows immediately on the same line.

stem: Type what the command prints (the three words are separated by single spaces).
explanation: Double quotes and no quotes expand the variable, so two of the words become `1`. Single quotes keep `$x` literal.
